function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

**Java – an overview** | Topic | What you’ll find | |-------|------------------| | **What it is** | Java is a high‑level, class‑based, object‑oriented programming language designed to have as few implementation dependencies as possible. It was originally developed by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems (now owned by Oracle Corporation) and released in 1995. | | **Key design goals** | • *Write once, run anywhere* (WORA): compiled bytecode runs on any device equipped with a Java Virtual Machine (JVM).
• Platform independence via JVM abstraction.
• Strong memory safety and automatic garbage collection.
• Robust standard library (the “Java Standard Edition” APIs).
• Built‑in support for multithreading and networking. | | **Typical uses** | • Enterprise back‑end services (Spring Boot, Jakarta EE)
• Android mobile apps (though Kotlin has largely taken over)
• Desktop GUI applications (Swing, JavaFX)
• Big‑data processing frameworks (Apache Hadoop, Apache Spark)
• Embedded systems & IoT devices
• Game development (LibGDX, jMonkeyEngine) | | **Core concepts** | - **Classes / Objects:** Encapsulation of state + behavior.
- **Inheritance & Polymorphism:** Code reuse and dynamic dispatch.
- **Interfaces & Abstract Classes:** Define contracts without concrete implementations.
- **Generics:** Type safety at compile time.
- **Annotations:** Metadata for code generation, configuration, etc.
- **Exception Handling:** Checked vs unchecked exceptions.
- **Concurrency utilities:** `java.util.concurrent` package provides thread pools, futures, locks, atomic variables, etc. | | **Compilation flow** | Source (`*.java`) → Compiler (`javac`) → Bytecode (`*.class`) → Runtime (`java` command/JVM). The JVM interprets or just‑instantly compiles this bytecode into native machine instructions per platform. | | **Ecosystem** | • **Build tools:** Maven, Gradle, Ant.
• **Testing frameworks:** JUnit, TestNG, Mockito.
• **Dependency management:** Central repositories like Maven Central, JCenter.
• **IDE’s:** IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse, NetBeans.
• **Community & standards bodies:** Java Community Process (JCP), open source projects. | | **Evolution** | Since Java SE 8 introduced lambda expressions and streams, newer releases keep adding modern language features (records, sealed classes, pattern matching, modules, var handles, project Loom fibers, Project Valhalla inline classes, etc.). | ### Quick example ```java public class HelloWorld { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("Hello, world!"); } } ``` Compile: ```bash $ javac HelloWorld.java # produces HelloWorld.class $ java HelloWorld # prints: Hello, world! ``` --- #### Bottom line Java is a mature, versatile, and widely adopted programming language whose core philosophy—platform neutrality through the JVM—is still very much alive today. Its rich ecosystem makes it suitable for everything from small scripts to massive distributed systems.
